Hot take

Yen intervention and UST

While Bessent helping the intervention on the yen and the change in language to "change" narrative is expanding with bloomberg reports and now an NYT article it's all trash. 

Mostly because The BOJ and MOF are managing the economic conditions of Japan. 

That statement is orders of magnitude more important than the consequences of the that policy on U.S. Treasury long term interest rates.

BOJ and MOF are dealing with an economy that is sputtering to expand and where imported energy creates inflationary vulnerability. The currency weakness is both caused by this economic conditions AND a cause of inflationary pressure when energy is purchased with Yen. Monetary policy is quite easy and the pace of yikes is being done in tiny incremental steps. Intervening in the currency market is a long tradition of the MOF particularly when market participants are way way over their skis short JPY. 

While the bond market regularly frets about JPY strength for two primary reasons one is practically irrelevant and the other is small in today's world

1. Under no circumstances will this intervention period require large sales of longer term UST. The MOF has hundreds of billions of cash like usd and perhaps a trillion of highly pledgable collateral if they want to borrow USD to support the yen without needing to sell a single bit of duration or FIMA programs 

2. Some interventions not only disrupt short term yen shorts but also create a carry trade unwind. People remember August 5th 2024 and think a carry trade unwind is a risk. But they forget that the carry trade unwind was caused by the assets financed in yen cratering NOT the yen causing an unwind. For what it's worth the performance of all risky assets since the intervention almost guarantee that the intervention didn't cause any pain whatsoever in the yen carry trade. 

The point being the US yield curve was NOT threatened by the yen intervention. The yen intervention was domestic decision which caused no concern nor consequence to the U.S. Bessent is just using this moment to tighten his relationship with a key long term investor in USD direct investment and equities and at some level bonds. It's symbolic at best.

Morpho vaults pay less than the markets they lend into.

The gap is the curator's fee. Fair deal, honestly. They pick the markets and watch the risk so you don't have to.

Kinda like travel agents. Paying someone to hunt down your flights made sense when the alternative was calling airlines one by one.

But it's a job you can do yourself.

If you cut the middle man & lend to the markets directly, you keep the whole rate.

It sounds easy, but then you open the @Morpho app.

Every market is its own research project with Different collateral, different oracle, different liquidity, different rate curve.

Ten tabs deep, you do what everyone does... sort by APY and ape the top row.

That's how you end up in a market paying 10%+ where 90% of the pool is already lent out. The rate is high BECAUSE nobody can leave. You're getting paid extra to be the guy stuck at the exit.

I went down this rabbit hole after my PT-reUSD post and found a tool called @monarchlend that makes everything so much easier.

It's basically Google Flights for Morpho markets. Makes everything so much easier and visual. 

It sorts everything in one table. You can see the APY, target rate, utilization, collateral, oracle, side by side. Filter by asset, liquidity, and risk guards.

Some markets pay more because borrower demand is real. Some pay more because the exit's crowded. You can tell which is which before your money's in it.

Watch these 3 things before you lend:

1/ The target rate. Today's APY is a snapshot. Every market drifts back to its target over time. A big gap between the two means you're chasing a spike, and spikes fade once fresh money shows up.

2/ Your exit. Utilization shows how much of the pool is already out the door. The closer it gets to 100%, the better the rate looks and the harder it is to leave.

3/ The collateral. You're lending against whatever borrowers posted. If you can't explain where its yield comes from, or it'd be ugly to liquidate, the APY doesn't matter.

You can find the 1st two with Monarch, but you gotta research the risks yourself.

In a bear market, every % matters.

And if you're the DIY type, you're already doing the curator's job anyway. Might as well keep their fee too.

I updated my 2023 roadmap diagram to overlay where the items that were there sit in the current Strawmap ( https://t.co/I35mrXutP2 ).

In general, a lot of overlap, but:

* Some things got reshuffled in order (eg. quantum safety up-prioritized)
* Some things deprioritized (eg. VDFs; many EVM improvements)
* Some things replaced with superior constructions (eg. Verkle -> unified BT -> PBT; state expiry -> new state types)

What's most striking, however, is that some completely new things are in the strawmap that are NOT in this diagram, because they were not in the 2023 roadmap at all. These reflect changing priorities.

Notably:

* First-class attention to strong privacy. This covers: keyed nonces and recent roots, aspects of FOCIL, lean privacy pool & wormholes
* Aggressive scaling in the context of post-quantum. This covers: leanSPHINCS signatures and aggregation, zkzk frames (see https://t.co/ibrOpMxMfO )
* Lean-ification of the spec, to assist in formal verification (full FV of everything is only possible because of modern AI)
* Blob and gas futures (this idea just didn't exist back in 2023)
* Native rollups (SNARKs were nowhere near mature enough to even consider this back in 2023)
* A more open design space for the "future of the EVM". zkzk frames already implies that the protocol will expose to users some ISA that's not the EVM - current leading candidates are leanISA and RISC-V. These ISAs are more simple, modern and efficient than the EVM. Once they're there, why not expose them to developers everywhere? (And then, why not turn the EVM into being an IR on top of that ISA, instead of an enshrined feature massively complicating the base protocol?) Though much of the deeper exploration here is too early even for the strawmap.
* New state types are not just a replacement for expiry, they're a fundamentally different paradigm to how Ethereum does scaling

A common theme in scaling, found in both state types and zkzk frames (both new ideas), is that instead of trying to maximally scale ALL ethereum activity, we try to create specialized mechanisms that have more restrictive properties that make them more scaling-friendly, while supporting the heaviest loads incurred by users and applications today (eg. token transfers, swaps) and tomorrow (eg. privacy protocols).

The other common theme is treating STARKs and AI-accelerated FV as first-class objects, that we are okay betting the technical future of Ethereum on. There are recursive STARKs in many layers of the protocol, one particular primitive (the "aggregate to union verified dependencies" primitive) is expected to be used in *three* places in the protocol: EL, CL and DL. This can only be safe with formal verification, which is itself only feasible with modern AI tools.

In general, many steps forward in maturity. And a huge amount of hard work by many dozens of Ethereum researchers and developers on all of these features.

Ethereum will be quantum-safe. Ethereum will put users' privacy first. Ethereum will be secure. Ethereum will be censorship-resistant. Ethereum will be highly performant and scalable while satisfying the above. And Ethereum will be Lean.

Broadwood is not a short-term activist.

• Broadwood has been investing in $STAA for more than 30 years and has been its largest shareholder since 2007.

• Today, Broadwood owns roughly 32% of the company.

• $STAA is Broadwood’s second-largest holding, representing roughly 21% of its public equity portfolio.

• In the most recent quarter alone, Broadwood purchased more than 1 million additional $STAA shares, increasing its ownership even further.

• Few investors know $STAA better than Broadwood. They have followed the company for more than three decades, remained invested through multiple industry cycles and continue increasing their ownership today.

• Broadwood is led by Neal Bradsher and has built a reputation as a highly concentrated long-term investor.

• According to WhaleWisdom’s estimated average purchase prices, Broadwood accumulated $MNST at an estimated average cost of roughly $3 per share. Today, $MNST trades around $90.

• WhaleWisdom also estimates Broadwood’s average purchase price in $AXON at roughly $26 per share. Today, $AXON trades around $520.

• Another major long-term investment was $QCOR, which was ultimately acquired by Mallinckrodt.

• Broadwood never argued that $STAA should not be sold. Their argument was that $30.75 per share was simply the wrong price at the wrong point in the cycle.

• Alcon approached $STAA regarding a potential acquisition.

• Alcon agreed to acquire $STAA for $28 per share in cash.

Broadwood wrote:

“While we are not opposed to a sale of the Company in principle, we were disappointed that STAAR’s Board of Directors made the consequential decision in August 2025 to sell the Company to Alcon at what we believe was a uniquely inopportune time, at a price that does not reflect the intrinsic value of the business and following a hasty and limited sale process.”

• Alcon increased its offer to $30.75 per share.

• The process unnecessarily limited participation from logical strategic buyers.

• Broadwood believed that a properly conducted process, after the operational recovery, could attract additional bidders and result in a materially higher valuation.

• Broadwood made clear it was not opposed to selling the company, but believed a sale should be evaluated after the turnaround, from a position of strength rather than weakness.

• UBS initiated coverage with a Sell rating and a $20 price target.

UBS’s bear case is straightforward:

• China may grow only 6-7%, below the roughly 10% expected by the Street.

• China still represents roughly half of $STAA’s revenue.

• LASIK remains deeply entrenched in the U.S.

• EVO ICL is more expensive than LASIK.

• Surgeons have limited economic incentive to switch.

• U.S. adoption may therefore remain slower than many investors expect.

These are all reasonable concerns. But none of them are new. China competition was already known. Weak U.S. penetration was already known. LASIK competition was already known. Higher ICL pricing was already known. Limited visibility in China was already known.

In other words, every major point in the UBS bear case already existed when Alcon was willing to pay $30.75 per share.

The difference today is that the business itself is materially stronger. Revenue has accelerated, margins have improved, profitability has improved and execution has improved. Yet the stock trades around $24, roughly 22% below the rejected acquisition offer.

Back then, the market had largely given up on the company. Analysts were cutting targets, sentiment was terrible and the stock was being sold aggressively.

At the same time, the people who arguably knew the business best, the founders/insiders-were doing the exact opposite. They were buying.

Over the following months, $WGS appreciated roughly 90%.

I’m not saying $STAA will follow the same path. Nobody knows.

𝗗𝗘𝗖𝗘𝗠𝗕𝗘𝗥 𝟴𝗧𝗛, 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱
Broadwood’s Open Letter to STAAR Surgical Shareholders

Broadwood wrote:

“While we are not opposed to a sale of the Company in principle, we were disappointed that STAAR’s Board of Directors made the consequential decision in August 2025 to sell the Company to Alcon at what we believe was a uniquely inopportune time, at a price that does not reflect the intrinsic value of the business and following a hasty and limited sale process.”

𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝟭𝟳, 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱

• Alcon increased its offer to $30.75 per share.

Broadwood still rejected the offer.

Their reasoning is worth revisiting.

Broadwood argued the company was being sold at the wrong point in the cycle, when earnings were temporarily depressed rather than normalized.

Broadwood also argued the sale process itself was fundamentally flawed.

According to Broadwood:

• The Board failed to run a competitive sale process.

• The process unnecessarily limited participation from logical strategic buyers.

• Broadwood stated it was aware of at least one additional strategic buyer that had expressed interest but was not given a meaningful opportunity to participate.

• Broadwood believed that a properly conducted process, after the operational recovery, could attract additional bidders and result in a materially higher valuation.

• Broadwood made clear it was not opposed to selling the company, but believed a sale should be evaluated after the turnaround, from a position of strength rather than weakness.

𝗝𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲

• Shareholders voted down the acquisition.

Then something interesting happened.

The business started improving.

𝗤𝟭 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲

Revenue increased to more than $90 million, versus roughly $68 million a year earlier. Gross margins improved, operating margins improved and profitability returned much faster than many investors expected.

𝗠𝗮𝘆 𝟭𝟭, 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲

Point72 Asset Management, Steven Cohen’s hedge fund, disclosed a 5.2% stake in $STAA at an average price of $29. The filing showed ownership of approximately 2.59 million shares. 

Part 1/2

Part 2/2

𝗤𝟮 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲

Preliminary revenue again exceeded expectations, reinforcing that the recovery was not just a one-quarter event.

The business today is materially stronger than it was when the $30.75 offer was made.

𝗝𝘂𝗹𝘆 𝟮𝟴, 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲

• UBS initiated coverage with a Sell rating and a $20 price target.

UBS’s bear case is straightforward:

• China may grow only 6-7%, below the roughly 10% expected by the Street.

• China still represents roughly half of $STAA’s revenue.

• LASIK remains deeply entrenched in the U.S.

• EVO ICL is more expensive than LASIK.

• Surgeons have limited economic incentive to switch.

• U.S. adoption may therefore remain slower than many investors expect.

These are all reasonable concerns. But none of them are new. China competition was already known. Weak U.S. penetration was already known. LASIK competition was already known. Higher ICL pricing was already known. Limited visibility in China was already known.

In other words, every major point in the UBS bear case already existed when Alcon was willing to pay $30.75 per share.

The difference today is that the business itself is materially stronger. Revenue has accelerated, margins have improved, profitability has improved and execution has improved. Yet the stock trades around $24, roughly 22% below the rejected acquisition offer.

This reminds me a little of $WGS.

Back then, the market had largely given up on the company. Analysts were cutting targets, sentiment was terrible and the stock was being sold aggressively.

At the same time, the people who arguably knew the business best, the founders/insiders-were doing the exact opposite. They were buying.

Over the following months, $WGS appreciated roughly 90%.

I’m not saying $STAA will follow the same path. Nobody knows.

What I do find interesting is that the pattern looks familiar. The tweet attached below was written when $ZIM was trading at $13.20.

At the time, there were already very credible reports that CEO Eli Glickman was interested in buying the company.

$ZIM had around $22 per share in cash.

Yet some analysts still had a Sell rating and a $6 price target.

Think about that.

$13.20 stock price.
$23 per share in cash.
Credible reports that the CEO wanted to buy the company.
And somehow the conclusion was $6.

It is also important to remember who writes many of the analyst reports we read.

A lot of them are written by people in their 20s or third-rate analysts who end up covering a niche industry involving companies in countries they only knew existed because they read about them in the newspaper.

They know how to build Excel models, project cash flows five years into the future and calculate a price target to the second decimal.

But investing also requires judgment and common sense.

And those future cash flow models often end up looking nothing like reality.

Then came the stupidity from the other side.

After the takeover deal was announced, $ZIM jumped close to $30.

Soon after, serious opposition started coming from Israel, including from government agencies, politicians and people who actually have influence over whether the deal can go through.

Yet mostly X users who have no clue what is actually happening in Israel suddenly decided they knew how the deal was going to end.

They somehow believed their opinion from X was more important than the position of the people who actually have a say in approving the deal.

That is a complete lack of common sense, mixed with a level of stupidity that I’m not sure is curable.

This is what investing often comes down to.

At $13.20, the market was ignoring what was directly in front of it.

Near $30, many investors were doing exactly the same thing, just in the opposite direction.

I still see almost no chance that this deal goes through.

And if $ZIM falls significantly when the deal falls apart, I believe it could become a great opportunity again, especially considering current shipping rates and the cash on the balance sheet.

Sometimes you don’t need a more complicated model.

You just need common sense.

Ethereum can't run on vibes, good intentions, or simple mission statements. not at it current size, scope, and scale

as a network with permissionless participation, it MUST run on incentives

in fact, it has always run on incentives. but "users" used to be more of a monolith than they are now, so wielding the threat of user consensus as a check on network operators is now qualitatively different

but network operators (now stakers) have never had more in common with vanilla holders of ETH. while the latter may not earn yield on their ETH, both are laser aligned with wanting to see the value of ETH appreciate.

where do users who hold only minimal ETH sit? well, you can infer that it is within the incentives for both stakers/operators and holders of ETH to grow and promote healthy network activity, and that means happy users. in fact, they have a much stronger incentive to promote this than even core devs do!

imo, it's best to be completely honest about these things. trying to obfuscate or ignore these dynamics will only lead to very, very bad things happening (like contentious hard forks)

while i believe in the mission of Ethereum, i'm a realist and i am an advocate for honest discussion which recognizes the actual environment in which it operates- not the environment people wish it operates in

it is the only thing which will make Ethereum anti-fragile for the longterm
